say.text: A 40-year-old is pulled from a house fire. Flame burns cover his face and neck. He is hoarse, and there is soot around his mouth.
You have just taken over his care. What is your first step?

choices.label: Work out the Parkland volume from the burn size
Secure the airway and give high-flow 100% oxygen
Watch the airway, intubate only if it fails
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which letter of ABCDE is most at risk in a burn to the face and neck, and which one comes first?
Starting with the fluid sum is the tempting model: a big burn feels like a fluid problem, so the Parkland sum comes to mind first.
Not yet. Burn sizing belongs to the secondary survey, which comes after the primary survey has checked the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at this one again: the sum is never the first move. The primary survey comes first.

say.text: Waiting is the tempting model: the airway sounds fine right now, so intubation can wait until it clearly fails.
That fails here. Early intubation is decided before the swelling closes the airway, on signs that predict it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: waiting for the airway to fail is the trap. Act on the warning signs.

say.text: Oedema builds after the burn, and an airway you could intubate now may not be intubatable later. So the airway is decided first, and the fluid sum waits.
Yes. Primary survey first: A for airway, with high-flow 100% oxygen while you assess.
Think of ABCDE as a ladder. You do not step up to the fluid sum before the airway is secure.
Only after that is the burn sized by depth, total body surface area, age and inhalation injury.

choices.label: I was sure about the airway, skip ahead

say.text: An hour later the same man is still talking and sitting up. Nothing has been done to his airway yet.
Which finding would make you intubate now, before the oedema closes the airway?

choices.label: Hoarseness, stridor, or a deep burn across the neck
Nothing yet, wait until he struggles to breathe
Wait for the swelling to show on the next check
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which signs mean the swelling is starting, not which ones show the airway has already closed.
Waiting for distress is the tempting model: he is talking, so the airway seems safe for now.
Not right. Early intubation is for the warning signs, given before oedema closes the airway, not when distress shows.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: distress comes after the swelling has started. Know the warning signs.

say.text: Waiting for the swelling to show is the same model in another form: the decision is pushed back until the airway is already changing.
Not right. Oedema is what makes intubation hard, so you act on the signs that come before it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: by the time swelling shows on a check, the tube may be harder to place.

say.text: Stridor, hoarseness, deep facial or neck burns, extensive soot in the mouth, or a falling level of consciousness all predict swelling. Those are your triggers.
Yes. Hoarseness, stridor, deep facial or neck burns and soot in the mouth mean early intubation, before oedema develops.
Intubate on the warning signs, not on the distress that follows.
Another burn, another ward. A man is brought in hoarse and coughing black sputum, with burns across the front of his neck.
The fluid chart is ready. What is your first move?

choices.label: Start the Parkland drip, then look at the airway
Give fluids and watch; intubate if the airway closes
Secure the airway now, before the swelling closes it

say.text: Starting the drip first is the fluid-first model again, in a new form: the big burn makes the sum feel urgent.
Not yet. The airway is checked in the primary survey, before the burn is sized or the sum is started.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the sum waits for the airway. The primary survey comes first.

say.text: Giving fluids and watching is the wait model again: the airway seems safe until it closes.
Not right. Intubation is decided on the warning signs before oedema closes the airway, so this patient is intubated now.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a burn to the neck with a hoarse voice is a reason to act now.

say.text: Yes. Airway first, decided before the sum, because oedema can close the airway later.
Airway first, then the burn itself: how deep it is and how much of the body it covers.
